title: Lesion-Symptom Inference Trap
summary: Draw a localisation inference from one fictional case, then meet six complications one at a time. Your stated confidence is set against the most the evidence can carry.
learningObjectives: Explain why lesion evidence speaks to necessity rather than to what tissue does.
Name six specific reasons a region-to-symptom inference can go wrong.
Distinguish a claim about one person from a population claim about a region.
Explain why vascular co-occurrence does not average away as a lesion sample grows.
Separate deficits attributable to damaged tissue from those attributable to oedema and diaschisis.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native range, radio and button controls. The confidence slider announces '70 per cent confident in the general localisation claim' rather than a bare number. The schematic map is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a table that decodes every mark by letter, name and meaning; the gauge and the confidence trace are likewise hidden and paired with printed percentages and a full step-by-step table. The overshoot beyond the evidence ceiling is drawn as a dashed outline and also stated in a sentence, so nothing depends on colour. Map letters carry a page-coloured halo so they stay legible on any fill in either palette. Reveals and verdicts announce through the shell's polite live region. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers; heading levels do not skip; reduced motion and forced colours are handled; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Why 'damage here, difficulty there' is not 'this region does that': lesion extent, vascular territory, diaschisis, premorbid level, co-occurring damage and task demands
simulationNotes: One invented case with an invented history, an invented scan and invented testing. The confidence ceiling is a teaching device rather than a calculation: it encodes the judgement that a single case with a large multi-region lesion inside a systematic vascular territory, measured at two weeks, in a person of unknown premorbid level and possibly atypical language organisation, cannot carry a general claim about what a region does. It runs 50, 40, 32, 26, 21, 17, 12 across the referral and the six complications. The specific claim - that tissue in the damaged volume was necessary for fluent speech output in this person, at this time, on these tasks - is treated as remaining well supported throughout, and making that asymmetry visible is the purpose of the exercise. The map is a schematic of two rounded outlines with labelled ellipses; nothing is to scale and no real scan, image or template is reproduced. Anatomical terms are coarse public textbook vocabulary. No real patient, published case or clinical record is described, and nothing on the page diagnoses anybody or offers a prognosis.
